29.title: The talents (Matthew 25:14–30)
29.hook: two servants risk what they were given; the third buries his out of fear
29.howItsDone: Christians often read the parable of the talents as a call to use the gifts God has given them in service of others, and churches often preach on it when inviting people to volunteer or give.

segments.voice: Remember the pay line? One denarius, a day's pay, for the dawn crew and the five o'clock crew alike. Generosity isn't fair; it's better.

A rich man is leaving on a long journey. He calls in three servants and hands over his fortune: five talents to one, two to the next, one to the third. Each, the story says, according to his ability. The first two go straight out, trade, and double what they were given. The third walks to a quiet spot, digs a hole, and buries his. Safe. Nobody can steal it. A long time later the master comes home to settle accounts. Two servants walk in with double. The third walks in with dirt still on the coins.
screen: `FIVE, TWO, ONE.` → `TWO PUT IT TO WORK.` → `ONE DIGS A HOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise: a talent wasn't a skill. It was a large weight of silver, a fortune in coin. Even the one-talent servant was handed a fortune. The usual account is that our English word talent, meaning a gift or ability, grew out of this very story: Christians took the talents to mean the gifts God gives each person, and over time the word changed meaning. A story, so the account goes, rewrote a dictionary. The master says the same words to the first two, in the old King James Bible: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant." Then the third speaks, and he's honest about why: "I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth." He didn't waste it. He didn't steal it. He just couldn't bear the risk. And the ending is hard: his talent is taken and given away, and he's thrown out. Christians read this in more than one way. Some hear it about gifts: whatever you've been given, however small, is meant to be used, not hidden. Some read it about waiting: it sits among Jesus's stories of the end of the age, a call to stay faithful until he comes back. Some notice that the third servant calls the master a hard man, reaping where he never sowed, and ask whether this master is meant to be God at all. Churches hold these readings side by side. On one thing the story is clear: it won't praise burying what you were given.

30.title: The rich fool (Luke 12:16–21)
30.hook: a man plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night
30.howItsDone: Many Christians read this parable as a warning against greed and a call to generosity, and it's often preached alongside giving to the poor, tithing, or simplifying how they live.

segments.voice: A talent was a weight of silver, and the servant who buried his did it out of fear.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. Jesus won't referee. He tells a story instead. A rich man's land has a bumper year, more grain than his barns can hold. He lies awake, talking it over with himself. What shall I do? I know: I'll tear down my barns and build bigger ones. I'll store everything. Then I'll say to my soul: you're set for years. Eat, drink, enjoy. It's a good plan. Any financial advisor would sign off on it. And that same night, God speaks to him, for the only time in the story, and calls him a fool.
screen: `SPLIT THE INHERITANCE.` → `A BUMPER YEAR.` → `BIGGER BARNS.` → `THAT SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Hear him: my crops, my barns, my fruits, my goods, my soul. I, my and mine, again and again. Nobody else is in the plan: no family, no workers, no neighbor. He even talks to his own soul, as if it's the only one in the room. The old King James Bible gives his words: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." And the answer: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?" He isn't a thief or a cheat; the land just produced. Saving isn't the problem either: the Bible praises the ant for storing food. His mistake is quieter. He thinks the barn is his life. Jesus says it plainly just before the story: a man's life doesn't consist in the abundance of the things he owns. And fool here doesn't mean stupid; he's clearly clever. In the Bible a fool is someone who lives as if God weren't there. Whose? He's about to leave it all to someone else, which is exactly what the brother in the crowd was fighting over. Luke ends with one more line: so is anyone who stores up treasure for himself and isn't rich toward God. Christians have heard rich toward God as generosity, prayer, a life turned outward. Luke's answer, a few verses on, is simple: give.

31.title: The unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35)
31.hook: forgiven a fortune, he throttles a man who owes him pocket change
31.tomorrow: the Pharisee and the tax collector
31.howItsDone: Christians ask God's forgiveness and pledge to forgive others every time they pray the Lord's Prayer ("forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors"), and churches often read this parable when teaching about forgiveness and reconciliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday's fool wasn't stupid; he lived as if God weren't there, building bigger barns.

Peter thinks he's being generous. How many times do I have to forgive my brother? Seven times? Jesus says: not seven. "Until seventy times seven." Then he tells a story. A king is settling his accounts, and a servant is brought in who owes ten thousand talents. That's the talent from two days ago; ten thousand is a debt no servant could ever pay. The king orders him sold, with his wife and children. The servant falls on his knees and begs for time. The king, moved with compassion, doesn't give him time. He cancels the whole debt. In the street, the free man meets a fellow servant who owes him a hundred silver coins.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES? SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN.` → `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS.` → `THE WHOLE DEBT, CANCELED.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, he "took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." A hundred silver coins was real money; in the vineyard story, one coin was a day's wage. Next to what he'd just been let off, it's pocket change. And the other man falls down and begs with almost the same words: have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. That echo is the point. He hears his own prayer coming back at him, and doesn't recognize it. He has the man thrown in prison. The other servants, upset, go to the king. The king calls him back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" The ending is hard. The king hands him over to be punished until he pays, and Jesus says the Father will do the same to anyone who doesn't forgive from the heart. Christians don't soften that, but they often hear the warning as the flip side of the gift: mercy received is meant to keep moving. It's the shape of the Lord's Prayer: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. The Greek of Jesus's answer to Peter can be read as seventy times seven or seventy-seven, and translators still differ. Either way it means: stop counting. Some Christian teachers add that forgiving a debt doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen, or staying where you'll be hurt. It means letting go of the throat.

32.title: The Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14)
32.hook: one prays about his own virtues; the other stands far off and asks only for mercy
32.howItsDone: Christians pray short, honest prayers in their own words, and Orthodox Christians often repeat the Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner"), which tradition traces to the tax collector's plea.

segments.voice: Ten thousand talents forgiven, then a hand on a throat over a hundred coins. Mercy is meant to keep moving.

Two men walk up to the temple in Jerusalem to pray. The first is a Pharisee. He stands and prays about himself. God, thank you that I'm not like other people. Not a cheat, not a crook, not unfaithful. Not like that tax collector back there. I fast twice a week. I give a tenth of everything I get. The second man is that tax collector. He won't come close. He stands far off, won't even lift his eyes, and beats his own chest. He says one sentence. Then Jesus says which of the two went home right with God.
screen: `TWO MEN GO UP TO PRAY.` → `ONE LISTS HIS VIRTUES.` → `ONE STANDS FAR OFF.`

segments.voice: Be fair to the Pharisee first; the story only works if you are. Pharisees were serious about God's law, and respected for it. This man isn't a fake, and the story never says he's lying. His fasting and giving are real devotion, and his prayer starts well, with thanks. Then it turns: "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are." One eye on God, one eye on the man at the back. The whole prayer is a comparison. Now the tax collector. Tax collectors gathered money for the rulers of the land, and the Pharisee's own prayer files this one next to extortioners. His prayer in the old King James is seven words: "God be merciful to me a sinner." No list. No comparison. Just the truth, said once. And Jesus says: "this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." Justified means made right. Luke tells us who the story was for: people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and looked down on everyone else. Not Pharisees. Anyone. Which sets a trap: the moment you think, thank God I'm not like that Pharisee, you've prayed his prayer. The tax collector's line has had a long life. Orthodox Christians trace the Jesus Prayer to it: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Monks and grandmothers say it over and over, quietly, through the day. Read this way, the story makes a quiet promise: an honest sentence is enough to bring.

33.title: The persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8)
33.hook: a widow wears down an unjust judge simply by never stopping
33.howItsDone: Some Christians keep praying for the same person or need for months or years, sometimes on a written list, and churches often pray for the same people week after week until something changes.

segments.voice: Justified: made right with God, the way the tax collector went home after one honest sentence.

There's a judge in a certain city, and Jesus sums him up in one line: he doesn't fear God, and he doesn't care what anyone thinks. You can't appeal to his conscience, and you can't shame him. And there's a widow in the same city, with no husband to speak for her and no money to smooth things along. Someone has wronged her, and she wants justice. She goes to the judge. He says no. She comes back. He ignores her. Every time the court sits, there she is. Finally the judge says to himself: I still don't fear God or care about anybody, but this woman is wearing me out. Give her what she wants.
screen: `A JUDGE WHO FEARS NOBODY.` → `A WIDOW WITH NOBODY.` → `SHE KEEPS COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Luke gives the point before the story starts: Jesus told it to show "that men ought always to pray, and not to faint." Not to faint means not to lose heart. And the thing to get right: the judge is not a picture of God. The story works by contrast. If a crooked judge who cares about nobody finally gives in to someone who won't stop asking, how much more will God, who does care, hear the people who cry out day and night? Jewish teachers had a name for this kind of argument: from the lesser to the greater. Now the funny part, hidden in the Greek. When the judge worries she'll weary him, Luke uses a word from the boxing ring: to hit under the eye, to give someone a black eye. He's half joking and half afraid. A widow with no power at all, and the man who runs the court is worried about his face. Widows matter here. Again and again the Hebrew Bible tells Israel to protect the widow, the orphan and the stranger, the people with no one to stand up for them. This widow has no one, so she stands up for herself, and doesn't stop. The story ends with a question, not a bow: "when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" As if the hard part isn't God listening. It's us still asking. Matthew's Gospel has Jesus say it another way: "knock, and it shall be opened unto you."

34.title: The great banquet (Luke 14:15–24)
34.hook: the invited guests make excuses, so the host fills the hall with the poor and the lame
34.howItsDone: Churches often run community meals, food pantries and open tables where anyone can eat, and some Christians make a point of inviting people who are usually left out.

segments.voice: A widow with no one to speak for her wore down a judge just by coming back.

Jesus is at dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, and a guest says, happily, how blessed will be the one who eats bread in the kingdom of God. Jesus answers with a dinner story. A man plans a great supper, invites many people, and they all say yes. When the food is ready, his servant goes out: come, it's ready. And one by one, they make excuses. I just bought a field, I have to go and see it. I just bought five pairs of oxen, I have to try them out. I just got married, so I can't come. The hall is set, the food is hot, and every chair is empty.
screen: `A GREAT SUPPER.` → `EVERYONE SAID YES.` → `EVERY CHAIR IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Some readers think the first listeners laughed out loud at those excuses. Who buys a field without seeing it, or ten oxen without testing them? These aren't reasons. They're ways of saying: I have better things to do. These guests had been invited ahead, said yes, and been called again when the meal was ready. Every one backed out at the last minute. The host is angry. He tells his servant: "Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind." People never invited anywhere. The servant comes back: there's still room. So the host sends him further, past the town to the roads and the hedges, where travelers and people with nowhere to go are, and says: "compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." Compel sounds harsh, but think who's being asked. Someone sleeping by a hedge, told a rich man wants him at dinner, might say: that can't be for me. He'd have to be talked into it. A few verses earlier, Jesus tells his own host the same thing: when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind, the people who can't invite you back. Christians often read the banquet as a picture of the kingdom of God: a table that stays set, where the empty chairs fill with people nobody expected. It's also about the ones asked first, who chose their fields instead.

35.title: The ten bridesmaids (Matthew 25:1–13)
35.hook: five bring spare oil for a groom who comes late; five run out
35.howItsDone: Many Christians hear this story in church in the weeks before Advent, when the readings turn to waiting and being ready, and some keep a habit of preparing the evening before for the day ahead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a host whose guests all made excuses compelled the people nobody invites to come in.

It's a wedding night in a village. Ten young women wait with their lamps to meet the groom and walk him in to the feast. Five brought a flask of spare oil. Five didn't. The groom is late. It gets dark, and all ten nod off. Then, at midnight, a shout: he's coming! Go out and meet him! They jump up and trim their lamps, and the five without spare oil watch their flames sputter. Give us some of your oil, they say, our lamps are going out. The other five say no. There might not be enough for all of us. Go and buy your own. So they run off into the night to find oil.
screen: `TEN LAMPS. A LATE GROOM.` → `MIDNIGHT: HE'S COMING.` → `FIVE LAMPS SPUTTER.`

segments.voice: Matthew places this story in the last days before Jesus's arrest. It's about waiting for someone who's late, and Christians have long read it as waiting for Christ to come again. The ending says so: "Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour." But look closer: "While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept." All ten. The wise ones fell asleep too. So the story isn't about staying on high alert every minute; nobody manages that. The difference was settled hours earlier, in daylight, when five of them thought: this might take longer than I expect. I'll bring a little extra. And the refusal to share? It sounds unkind. But some things can't be borrowed at the last minute, and readiness is one of them. At midnight you can't borrow someone else's years of practice, or their steadiness, or their prayers. While the five are off buying oil, the groom arrives, the ready ones go in with him, "and the door was shut." It's a hard ending, and the story doesn't soften it. The old King James calls them ten virgins; the Greek word means young unmarried women, which is why modern tellings say bridesmaids. Nobody's sure what their lamps were: small clay oil lamps, or torches wrapped in oily rags that burn out fast. Either way, the light only lasts as long as the oil.
screen: `WAITING FOR SOMEONE LATE` · `ALL TEN FELL ASLEEP` · `READINESS CAN'T BE BORROWED` · `THE DOOR WAS SHUT` · then, large: `YE KNOW NEITHER THE DAY NOR THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: Think about the first hour of tomorrow, and what tomorrow-you will wish you'd done tonight: the water bottle filled, the clothes laid out, the line for a hard conversation written down, the thing that always dies charged. Pick one small thing and picture yourself doing it calmly, without fuss; that's the spare flask. Then let it go, and rest here, the way all ten rested.
Virgins. The old King James word for the ten young women waiting with their lamps, five with spare oil and five without, for a groom who came late.
Your line: bring a little extra oil. That's week five, from the buried talent to the oil. Tomorrow, the last parable.
